# macOS post-office boot service

A post office that must survive a reboot runs as a **LaunchDaemon**, with
`RunAtLoad` and `KeepAlive`. The older LaunchAgent runs only in the logged-in
user's GUI session: it does not run before login or after logout and does not
satisfy unattended boot. The daemon plist is owned by
root, but `UserName` runs the node as the ordinary service user. The encrypted
keystore, password file, and relay log remain in
`~/.local/share/mesh-talk-post-office`; logs are in
`~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office`. Never replace an existing password
file or keystore during an update.

The service must use `--password-file`; never put the keystore password in
`--password` process arguments or in a plist. The installer sets the data
directory to mode `700` and its password file to owner-only mode `600`.

## Build, install, and update

From the desired source revision on a Mac, build the Intel release binary with
the same stable toolchain for Cargo and rustc:

```bash
rustup target add --toolchain stable x86_64-apple-darwin
RUSTC="$(rustup which --toolchain stable rustc)" \
  "$(rustup which --toolchain stable cargo)" build --locked --release \
  --target x86_64-apple-darwin -p mesh-talk-core --bin mesh-talk-node
file target/x86_64-apple-darwin/release/mesh-talk-node
```

For Apple Silicon, use `aarch64-apple-darwin` for both the target and artifact
path. The repository's `scripts/install-post-office-macos.sh` has two phases:

1. As the service user, run `prepare` with a staged binary, relay name and
   ports. It verifies the binary, preserves existing identity and queued mail,
   creates a password only for a new relay, and writes a private staged plist.
2. Interactively run `activate` on that Mac. It asks for administrator
   authorization, installs a root-owned plist in `/Library/LaunchDaemons`,
   stops the old per-login agent if present, and starts the boot service.

Managed post offices use dedicated UDP **47478** on every host and also
participate on shared LAN UDP **47474**. The installer supplies both defaults
and fixes the main TCP listener at **47479**. Preparation and activation reject
other main TCP or discovery ports before changing service state. Desktop
apps use UDP 47474; routed inventories probe both role ports. Different hosts
are distinguished by IP, so their post offices do not need different ports.
The raw CLI permits custom ports for isolated test networks; those endpoints
require explicit discovery and are outside the managed deployment contract.
The signed discovery response advertises TCP 47479. Optional legacy gateways
use a separate TCP listener; their port must differ from the main listener.

Example for the Intel relay on LAN X (paths and addresses are deployment-specific):

```bash
ssh mac2015 'install -d -m 700 "$HOME/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office"'
scp target/x86_64-apple-darwin/release/mesh-talk-node scripts/install-post-office-macos.sh relays.conf mac2015:~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/
ssh mac2015 'bash ~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/install-post-office-macos.sh prepare \
  --binary ~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/mesh-talk-node \
  --name mac2015-post-office --port 47479 --discovery-port 47478 \
  --lan-announce-port 47474 --bridge \
  --federation-config ~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/relays.conf'
ssh -tt mac2015 'bash ~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/install-post-office-macos.sh activate'
```

For an update, repeat the build, transfer, `prepare`, and `activate` commands
with the same service user, ports, name, and trust manifest. `prepare` installs
and validates `~/.local/bin/mesh-talk-node.next`, then replaces the binary with
`mv`; `activate` restarts the daemon. It preserves the existing password,
keystore, and queued relay data. If existing state has no password file, recover
the original password instead of creating a new relay identity.

`prepare` also preserves the installed executable's code-signing identifier
when updating an ad hoc or unsigned local build. A first local installation uses
`com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.node`. Publisher-issued signatures are preserved,
and signature verification must succeed before the installed executable is
replaced. The code-signing identifier is separate from the cryptographic relay
device ID: both need continuity, but preserving the keystore alone does not
preserve macOS's local-network permission tracking. See Apple's
[local network privacy guidance](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3179-understanding-local-network-privacy).

Use `prepare` for updates rather than copying a freshly linked executable over
the installed binary. After restarting, check actual LAN discovery as well as
the TCP listener and routed signed query. A running service or a successful
Tailscale connection does not prove that LAN multicast is working. If an older
manual update changed the signing identifier, preserve the identifier from the
known working binary backup when preparing the repair; do not disable
system-wide local-network privacy.

Example for the reciprocal relay on another LAN:

```bash
scp target/aarch64-apple-darwin/release/mesh-talk-node mac2015:~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/mesh-talk-node-arm
ssh mac2015 'scp ~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/mesh-talk-node-arm mac-mini:/Users/stella/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/'
ssh mac2015 'scp ~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/install-post-office-macos.sh ~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/relays.conf mac-mini:~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/'
ssh -tt mac2015 'ssh -tt mac-mini bash /Users/stella/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/install-post-office-macos.sh prepare \
  --binary /Users/stella/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/mesh-talk-node-arm \
  --name mac-mini-post-office --port 47479 --discovery-port 47478 \
  --lan-announce-port 47474 --bridge \
  --federation-config /Users/stella/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/relays.conf'
ssh -tt mac2015 'ssh -tt mac-mini bash /Users/stella/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/install-post-office-macos.sh activate'
```

Both commands use the same public manifest; each host keeps its own private
identity and listener configuration. Preparation validates the manifest and
copies it to `~/.local/share/mesh-talk-post-office/federation.conf`; the daemon
uses that persistent absolute path. Enrollment/revocation changes require
redistributing the updated file and restarting every affected relay. A file edit
alone does not revoke running sessions. Existing `--federation-peer` flags remain
supported when no manifest is supplied.

If the only physical route between two sites fails, the local relay retains
encrypted outgoing mail within its retention and capacity limits until a route returns.

## Approved network membership

To use automatic member discovery instead of a shared pin list, issue this
relay's membership on the offline enrollment workstation using the
[network administration workflow](post-office-federation.md#automatic-membership-in-an-approved-network).
Keep its existing device identity and password. Prepare with `--relay-network
/path/network.policy --relay-membership /path/relay.membership`, optionally
repeating `--relay-seed <fingerprint>@<ip>:47478` for routed sites. These replace
`--federation-config`/`--federation-peer` and a legacy gateway; no explicit
`--bridge` is needed. Preparation verifies public approval before changing
installation state and persists both public files beside the relay keystore.
The daemon uses their absolute paths after staging files are removed. Use the
existing interactive `activate` step to restart the service after policy changes
or certificate renewal. Never install `authority.key` on a relay. Preparation
validates the certificate's public approval; startup additionally verifies it
matches the loaded persistent device identity before opening network listeners.

## Migrate the legacy LaunchAgent

The old job is `gui/<service-user-uid>/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office`;
its plist is
`~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office.plist`.
Inspect it as the service user in that user's logged-in GUI session:

```bash
launchctl print "gui/$(id -u)/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office" 2>/dev/null || true
if [ -f "$HOME/Library/LaunchAgents/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office.plist" ]; then
  plutil -lint "$HOME/Library/LaunchAgents/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office.plist"
fi
```

`prepare` writes `~/.local/state/mesh-talk-post-office/LaunchDaemon.plist`;
`activate` installs it at
`/Library/LaunchDaemons/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office.plist` and
unloads the old GUI job. After verifying the system job below, remove the old
agent plist so the next GUI login cannot load a competing relay:

```bash
launchctl bootout "gui/$(id -u)/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office" 2>/dev/null || true
rm -f "$HOME/Library/LaunchAgents/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office.plist"
```

## Check and operate

Check boot-service state, credentials, and listeners as the service user:

```bash
sudo launchctl print system/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office
lsof -nP -iTCP:47479 -sTCP:LISTEN
lsof -nP -iUDP:47478
shasum -a 256 ~/.local/bin/mesh-talk-node
chmod 600 "$HOME/.local/share/mesh-talk-post-office/password"
stat -f '%Su %Sp %N' "$HOME/.local/share/mesh-talk-post-office" "$HOME/.local/share/mesh-talk-post-office/password"
```

The owner must be the service user; permissions must be `drwx------` on the
data directory and `-rw-------` on the password file. The daemon plist contains
the password file's absolute path, never the secret. To restart the installed
service after an update or configuration change:

```bash
sudo launchctl kickstart -k system/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office
sudo launchctl print system/com.octopusgarage.mesh-talk.post-office
```

The LaunchDaemon restarts the process after a crash and after boot, before a
user logs in. Tailscale availability is separate: a relay may start before its
VPN is ready, and its federation loop retries until the routed path returns. To
verify an actual reboot, restart one machine at a time and recheck the system
launchd job, signed discovery, configured listeners, and an encrypted message.

Relays see authenticated device/IP connections, pseudonymous mailbox and event
IDs, timing, counts, and size buckets; trusted federation peers can correlate
the same mailbox across sites. Legacy relay-specific queues do not replicate.
Version-3 federation reconciles reachable trusted relays opportunistically;
using several relays does not guarantee replicated custody or delivery after a
route loss. See [relay metadata privacy](post-office-metadata-privacy.md) for
trust, retention, and deletion limits.

## Cross-machine delivery test

From a Mac on the same LAN, build the CLI with `cargo build -p mesh-talk-core
--bin mesh-talk-node`, take the relay device ID from its startup line, then run:

```bash
python3 scripts/e2e-post-office-lan.py --ssh-host mac2015 --relay-id <relay-device-id>
python3 scripts/e2e-post-office-lan.py --ssh-host mac2015 --relay-id <relay-device-id> --file-roundtrip
python3 scripts/e2e-post-office-lan.py --ssh-host mac2015 --relay-id <relay-device-id> --multi-relay
```

The test creates disposable Alice and Bob identities, checks discovery of the
installed relay, sends a DM and a private channel event while Bob is offline,
stops Alice, and restarts Bob to verify
both deliveries. It leaves the installed relay identity and queued data intact.
The file roundtrip variant proves that the offer reaches Bob through the
installed relay after Alice stops. This older harness queries Bob's local
attachment consent when Alice returns and transfers the bytes while both peers
are online; that overlap is a harness limitation, not a current protocol
requirement. The Python file roundtrip does not prove that file bytes crossed
the relay.

The Python `--restart-relay-before-drain` switch restarts the legacy
`gui/<uid>/...` job. The ignored mac2015 Rust test also defaults to that job;
select `MESH_TALK_E2E_MAC2015_SERVICE=system` for the current LaunchDaemon.
Only `system` and `legacy-agent` are accepted selector values.

```bash
python3 scripts/e2e-post-office-lan.py --ssh-host mac2015 --relay-id <relay-device-id> --restart-relay-before-drain
MESH_TALK_E2E_MAC2015_RELAY_ID=<relay-device-id> cargo test -p mesh-talk-core --lib mac2015_post_office_delivers_file_bytes_after_both_peers_go_offline -- --ignored --nocapture
```

The ignored Rust LAN test covers that final handoff. It discovers the signed
announcement from the installed mac2015 relay, keeps Bob offline while Alice
uploads the file offer, then drains the offer and obtains Bob's authenticated
consent. It stops Bob before any chunks arrive, uploads the encrypted chunks to
mac2015, stops Alice, restarts the relay, and checks that Bob recovers the exact
file bytes. This is a deliberate test harness sequence: Bob must briefly be
online to approve the offer and answer Alice's direct consent query.

For the installed **system LaunchDaemon**, run the same Rust test explicitly
in system mode. Its SSH restart uses `sudo -n`; the SSH service user must already
have administrator authorization permitting that command noninteractively.
An interactive `sudo -v` in another SSH session does not necessarily authorize
this session. Confirm the site's approved sudo policy first; this test neither
prompts for nor transmits an administrator password. It restarts the installed
relay, so run it in an agreed service-maintenance window:

```bash
MESH_TALK_E2E_MAC2015_SERVICE=system \
MESH_TALK_E2E_MAC2015_RELAY_ID=<relay-device-id> \
  cargo test -p mesh-talk-core --lib \
  node::delivery_runtime_tests::mac2015_post_office_delivers_file_bytes_after_both_peers_go_offline \
  -- --ignored --exact --nocapture
```

## Troubleshooting

### Common Build Issues

#### Missing Dependencies

If you encounter missing dependencies during build:

```bash
# macOS
xcode-select --install

# Ubuntu/Debian
sudo apt update
sudo apt install libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev libgtk-3-dev libayatana-appindicator3-dev librsvg2-dev patchelf

# For other distributions, use the Tauri 2 prerequisites for your target.
```

#### Rust Compilation Errors

Update your Rust toolchain:

```bash
rustup update
```

#### Node.js Version Issues

Ensure you're using a compatible Node.js version:

```bash
node --version  # CI uses Node.js 22
```

### Runtime Issues

#### Application Won't Start

1. Check that all prerequisites are installed
2. Verify the application has necessary permissions
3. Check system logs for error messages

#### Network Discovery Not Working

1. Ensure UDP port 47474 (multicast group 224.0.0.167) is not blocked by firewall
2. For automatic LAN discovery, check that nodes share a local network segment;
   for routed or bridged discovery, check the configured network path and client
   opt-in in the [topology guide](../docs/network-topologies.md)
3. Verify that the network allows multicast/UDP between hosts (some guest/AP-isolated
   Wi-Fi blocks it); on macOS the app ships the `com.apple.developer.networking.multicast`
   entitlement so the OS permits multicast

#### Local Storage Issues

Mesh-Talk keeps protocol and account data as encrypted files under `~/.mesh-talk`.
Optional installed packs are kept separately in the webview's IndexedDB, and some
UI preferences use local storage. If an encrypted account store appears corrupt:

1. Close the application and preserve a copy of the affected data directory before
   attempting recovery. Keep the original encrypted stores and keys intact.
2. Record the error and check available disk space, file permissions and whether
   another process is using the profile. Do not remove an account directory as a
   general repair step.
3. If you have a verified `.mtbackup` archive and its matching recovery key, follow
   [backup and recovery](../docs/backup-recovery.md) to restore under an unused local
   username. Restore creates a new device; it does not repair or merge into the
   damaged profile or revoke its identity.

Peer synchronization can supply only retained, authorized content over an available
path. It cannot replace missing local keys or guarantee complete history or file
bytes. Keep the preserved profile for diagnosis if no verified recovery path is
available.

### Platform-Specific Troubleshooting

#### macOS

- If Gatekeeper prevents the app from opening:
  - Right-click the app and select "Open"
  - See the first-run instructions in the root README for an unsigned build

#### Windows

- If WebView2 is missing:

- If SmartScreen blocks the installer:
  - Click "More info" and then "Run anyway"

#### Linux

- If the AppImage won't run:

  - Or run with: `./mesh-talk.AppImage --no-sandbox`

# Local build retention

Managed Rust builds and tests share a machine-local retention policy. Successful
`make build` commands archive release binaries; `make tauri-build` archives the
newly generated native bundles. Keep the latest **five successful build sets**
across all registered checkouts and worktrees. Each set includes its commit,
branch, dirty-worktree status, source path, and timestamp.

After dependency bootstrap, the local health gate holds a managed checkout
lease across all build/test execution, including browser execution and the intervals between Cargo phases. Cargo's own compiler
lock ends before its test executables finish; it cannot protect a long test run
from scheduled cache eviction. The health supervisor uses the existing process
group cleanup contract and always runs the aggregate gate freshly, while its
individual stages retain their input-bound reuse. This protects checkout-local
targets through full health without disabling cleanup for other idle checkouts.

After a successful managed command, cleanup measures the combined Cargo targets
and evicts compiler caches from the least recently used checkout until usage is
at most **40 GiB**, where possible. A checkout's `deps`, `.fingerprint`, `build`,
`incremental`, and `examples` directories are evicted together within each idle
debug, release, or cross-compilation profile. Coverage profiles are also eligible.
Removing these caches makes the next affected build recompile; runnable binaries,
native bundles, documentation, source, and application data remain available.
The budget is soft when preserved files alone exceed it. Archived packages are
separate from the compiler-cache budget and have a count limit, not a byte limit.
Automatic cache scans run at most once every ten minutes; package retention is
checked after every successful managed command. Post-command cleanup also keeps
profiles whose cache files or verified managed-use marker were active within the
last **ten minutes**. This avoids repeatedly deleting a fresh cache when active
or preserved outputs already keep total usage above the soft budget. Older idle
profiles and worktrees remain eligible. Coordination lock timestamps do not count
as cache use, so cleanup itself cannot renew this window.

Manual and scheduled `clean` commands always scan and retain their immediate
budget policy; the automatic idle window does not apply to them. Active profiles
are skipped while cleanup continues through idle profiles and other worktrees.
An incomplete cleanup reports excess usage and does not advance the scan interval,
so the next successful command can retry immediately. The window reduces cache
churn during development; it does not increase the configured budget or guarantee
that scheduled cleanup will preserve a warm profile.

## Commands

Requires Python 3.11 or later and Git.

```sh
make clean-builds-dry-run
make clean-builds

# Register another clone; its worktrees are discovered automatically too.
python3 scripts/build-retention.py clean --checkout /path/to/another/mesh-talk

# Protect custom commands from concurrent cleanup.
python3 scripts/build-retention.py run -- cargo test -p mesh-talk-core --lib account_sync

# Opt out of the automatic idle window for this command.
python3 scripts/build-retention.py run --min-idle-seconds 0 -- cargo check -p mesh-talk-core
```

An explicit `--checkout` is remembered after a real cleanup run, including runs
below the budget. A dry-run reports the proposed deletions without registering
checkouts or changing caches, packages, or the deletion log. It may create the
state directory and Cargo coordination lock files. The registry lives outside Git, so every worktree
using the mechanism shares it. Old branches need these script/Makefile changes
before their builds acquire the managed lock.

Managed Make targets include `build`, `tauri-build`, `install-deps`, `test`,
`test-focused`, `e2e`, `lint`, `tauri-dev`, `clean`, and `check`. Direct Cargo
commands are still supported, but do not automatically trigger this policy.
`run` executes commands from the repository root. Failed commands preserve their
exit status and do not archive or trigger cleanup. Archive/cleanup failures print
a warning and preserve a successful build's exit status.

## Configuration

| Setting                                                      | Default                              | Meaning                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `MT_BUILD_KEEP` / `--keep`                                   | `5`                                  | Successful build sets to retain; at least one                                                                                        |
| `MT_BUILD_CACHE_GB` / `--budget-gb`                          | `40`                                 | Combined Cargo target budget in GiB                                                                                                  |
| `MT_BUILD_STATE_DIR`                                         | `~/.cache/mesh-talk/build-retention` | Shared archive, registry, locks, and log directory                                                                                   |
| `MT_BUILD_CHECKOUTS`                                         | empty                                | Additional clones, separated by the platform path separator                                                                          |
| `MT_BUILD_SCAN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` / `--interval-seconds`      | `600`                                | Minimum interval between automatic cache scans; `0` scans after every command                                                        |
| `MT_BUILD_CACHE_MIN_IDLE_SECONDS` / `run --min-idle-seconds` | `600`                                | Minimum idle time before post-command cache eviction; nonnegative; `0` disables the window; explicit/scheduled `clean` is unaffected |
| `MT_TARGET_CLEAN`                                            | `1`                                  | Set to `0` to disable eviction; successful builds can still be archived                                                              |

Archives are under `packages/`; `cleanup.jsonl` records deletion attempts with
paths, timestamps, and estimated bytes. Packages appear atomically after copying;
an interrupted copy remains hidden until a later cleanup removes it. The state
directory must remain outside all registered checkouts. Use one state directory
for all worktrees so their locks and retention counts are shared.

Archiving supports the native default `target/release` layout used by the Make
targets. Custom output locations, target triples, build directories, and profile
overrides skip automatic archiving and that command's cleanup with a warning.
Standalone cleanup only considers verified checkout-local `target/` directories;
external/custom target directories are not deletion candidates.

Managed commands refresh `.mesh-talk-build-use` in their checkout-local target.
An explicit `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` (or `CARGO_BUILD_TARGET_DIR` when it is unset) also
refreshes that target's marker when it is a verified Mesh Talk checkout's real
`target/` directory. This preserves a shared cache even when a Cargo cache hit
updates no artifacts. Unverified/external output directories and symlinked
markers are not written. The wrapper does not resolve command-line or Cargo
configuration-only output overrides, or separate build directories, into managed
markers; those inputs retain their existing output/archiving limitations. Recent
cache-file activity still receives the automatic window where the existing
collector owns that profile.

## Concurrency and scheduling

Managed builds hold one OS lock per checkout, protecting the command and package
capture. Cleanup skips that checkout if the lock is busy and continues through
other checkouts. A separate cleanup lock prevents overlapping collectors; a
package lock protects archive copies and retention. No machine-wide build lock
or process-name guard blocks unrelated idle worktrees.

Within an idle managed checkout, cleanup takes nonblocking exclusive locks on
each profile's `.cargo-lock`, `.cargo-build-lock`, and `.cargo-artifact-lock`.
These coordinate with raw Cargo invocations using both older and newer Cargo
locking layouts. A busy profile is preserved; idle sibling profiles can still
be cleaned. A Cargo build that starts during deletion waits on the profile lock.
Profile directories and lock files remain in place throughout cleanup.
The lock paths follow Cargo's
[1.95 layout](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/rust-1.95.0/src/cargo/core/compiler/layout.rs)
and [1.96 layout](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/blob/rust-1.96.0/src/cargo/core/compiler/layout.rs).
The fixture suite verifies mutual exclusion with a real installed Cargo process.

This mechanism targets local filesystems with working OS file locks. Unsupported
or failed locks preserve the affected profile. OS locks release automatically
when their owner exits. Symlinked targets, profiles, and lock files are excluded,
and cleanup does not follow symlinks inside compiler caches. Use managed Make
commands to protect the entire Tauri bundling lifecycle as well as compilation.

`make dev` installs a macOS launchd fallback that runs every ten minutes and at
03:00. Busy profiles are retried at the next interval,
including for older worktrees without post-build hooks. To update it directly:

```sh
./scripts/install-auto-clean-macos.sh
```

The installer copies the runner outside the checkout so switching branches does
not remove it, and captures the current configuration and PATH. Reinstall after
changing these settings or updating the runner. It operates on the same shared
registry as post-build cleanup. Logs go to
`~/Library/Logs/mesh-talk-target-gc.log`.

# Project-wide resource limits to keep cargo from saturating the CPU.
#
# Rationale: cargo sizes both compilation and test parallelism to the number of
# CPU cores by default, which pins all cores. (Test builds use cheap KDF params via
# cfg(test)/the fast-test-kdf feature, so the suite is no longer KDF-bound — but a
# full parallel compile can still saturate a small machine.) These caps apply to
# EVERY cargo invocation in this tree (CI, contributors, and AI sessions) automatically.
#
# Tuned for an 8-core machine at a "gentle" ~half-cores level. Adjust the two
# numbers if you change machines.

[build]
# Cap parallel compilation units (codegen jobs). ~half of logical cores.
jobs = 4

[env]
# Cap libtest's parallel test threads so the suite doesn't pin every core at once.
# Honored by the test harness produced by `cargo test`.
RUST_TEST_THREADS = "4"
inherits = "test"
debug = "none"
incremental = true

# Keep the default speed-oriented opt-level while reducing duplicate native code and
# shipping symbols. Thin LTO limits release build time compared with fat LTO.
[profile.release]
lto = "thin"
codegen-units = 1
strip = "symbols"

# The Tauri shell dominates local release rebuilds. Split only this crate's
# code generation across cores; keep dependencies and the protocol core at one
# unit for their existing release-size/runtime trade-off. Thin LTO and symbol
# stripping still apply to the final app.
[profile.release.package.mesh-talk]
codegen-units = 4
